title: Quantifying transport dynamics with three-dimensional single-particle tracking in adherent cells
protocol: Disassociate A549 cells as described in steps 3d–3g of the cell culture section.
Plate disassociated cells in glass-bottom Petri dishes containing 2 mL complete DMEM.
Incubate plates in a humidified incubator at 37°C and 5% CO2 for at least 24 hours.
Grow cells to achieve confluency between 50% and 60%, as observed by light microscopy.
Introduce fluorescent particles into cells using one of the three described methods.
Prewarm the stock solution containing 100-nm fluorescent beads at 37°C for approximately 10 min.
Centrifuge the stock solution in a microfuge at 5,000 × g for 3 min.
Aspirate 0.5 μL of the supernatant reagent using a pipette.
Mix the reagent with 2 mL of complete DMEM to achieve a final concentration of 9 × 10^6 microspheres/mL in a 15 mL centrifuge tube.
Pipette up and down at least 10 times to mix the liquid with the medium.
Replace the medium in the Petri dish with the mixed medium.
Culture the cells in an incubator for approximately 4 h.
Discard the medium and rinse the cell 3 times with 4 mL prewarmed PBS.
Incubate at least 10 min before imaging.
Label intracellular vesicles via endocytosis of EGFRs.
Cultivate cells in serum-free DMEM with 10 nM biotin-EGF on ice for 15 min.
Wash cells with cold PBS three times.
Incubate cells with 0.5–1 nM streptavidin-coated quantum dots for 5 minutes.
Wash cells with cold PBS three times to remove unlabeled streptavidin-QDs.
Transfer cells to 37°C for at least 1 hour before imaging.
Maintain osmotic pressure balance by culturing cells in a hypertonic solution mixed with fluorescent particles.
Incubate cells under conditions that allow vesicles containing the hypertonic solution and fluorescent particles to rupture, releasing fluorescent particles into the cytoplasm.
Make the hypertonic loading medium according to the protocol of pinocytic cell-loading reagent (I-14402).
Centrifuge the stock solution of fluorescent particles following steps 4a and 4b of the protocol.
Aspirate the supernatant after centrifugation.
Add approximately 0.2 μL of fluorescent particles to a 0.5 mL centrifuge tube containing 100 μL of hypertonic loading medium.
Discard the medium in the Petri dish.
Pipette the hypertonic medium containing the particles gently into the dish.
Culture for 10 minutes in the incubator.
Discard the hypertonic solution in the Petri dish.
Add 2 mL of hypotonic solution (serum-free medium and deionized water in a 6:4 ratio) to the dish.
Incubate for 2 minutes.
Add 20 mL distilled water to the bath of the incubator to keep the humidity.
Open the valve of the gas cylinder and the pressure relief valve in sequence to maintain the CO2 supply of the incubator.
Adjust the valve to set the pressure to be approximately 0.1 MPa.
Turn on the power of the incubation system.
Place an empty Petri dish in the chamber.
Set the temperature of the top heater, stage heater, bath heater, and lens heater to 37°C for half an hour before live cell imaging.
Turn on the 940 nm laser light source.
Turn on the piezoelectric stage.
Open the focus-locking software.
Adjust the initial position of the piezo stage at 50 μm.
Start the imaging of the infrared spot reflected by the interface between the specimen and coverglass.
Set the laser intensity for best imaging.
Set the gain for best imaging.
Set the exposure time for best imaging.
Set a threshold between 0–255 for 8-bit images.
Locate the centroid of imaged points using pixels with intensities above the threshold.
Set the step size of the piezo stage to 20 nm.
Set the sensitivity parameter to 1 pixel.
Click lock to start focus after setting the focal plane.
Place the dish in the observation chamber on the microscope.
Turn on the brightfield light source.
Look down the eyepieces to focus the sample.
Position on a region of interest.
Turn off the brightfield light source.
Choose a laser compatible with the fluorescent particles and start at moderate power.
Mix the weakest possible laser power to reduce photobleaching and avoid cell damage.
Use the appropriate optical path, open the shutter, and detect the fluorescent signal with the EMCCD.
Focus on the fluorescent particles on the bottom of the sample.
Adjust the illumination angle for HILO imaging.
Cool down the EMCCD to −75°C.
Set the camera exposure time at 30 ms.
Set the gain of the EMCCD between 0–300.
Select the frame transfer mode of the EMCCD.
Set the repeat to be 2,000 times.
Choose the stream mode to realize the fastest frame rates.
Select a cell containing fluorescent particles.
Take 2,000 frames of video.
Switch to brightfield illumination after taking the video.
Take a single snapshot of the cell.
Image immobilized particles under the same conditions as living cells.
Determine the localization precision of the imaging platform.
Take 2,000 frames of video of fixed particles.
Lift the lens in 50 nm steps every 5 seconds during imaging.
Finish imaging each sample within 2-4 hours.
Save all images in TIFF format for processing.
Reconstruct 3D trajectories from video using ImageJ and MATLAB.
Extract lateral trajectory from the focal plane through the ImageJ plugin particle tracker.
Determine axial coordinates by fitting the diffraction ring with a MATLAB script.
Select a region consisting of cells.
Duplicate the video of the selected region.
Save duplicated file for processing.
Open images using ImageJ, an open-source image analysis software program.
Adjust video brightness using the Image-Adjust-Brightness/Contrast tool in ImageJ.
Draw a rectangle around the region of interest containing cells on the focus plane with the Rectangle Tool.
Duplicate the image stack of the selected region using the Image-duplicate tool.
Move the rectangular region 256 pixels horizontally to the defocused plane using the Edit–Selection–Specify tool.
Duplicate the defocused image stack using the duplicate tool.
Save the duplicated stacks of the focused plane and defocused plane areas to a folder.
Create a new subfolder named “def”.
Use the File–Save As–Image sequence tool to save the defocused image stack in the folder “def” as an image sequence.
Set the stack's name to empty on the dialog screen.
Obtain the transformation matrix between the two planes.
Select at least three bright spots on the focused plane stack using the polygon selection tool.
Adjust the position of the polygon vertices approximately in the center of the bright spots with the magnifying glass tool.
Copy the polygon to the defocused plane stack using the Edit–Selection–Restore Selection tool.
Similarly, adjust the position of polygon vertices with the magnifying glass tool on the defocused plane.
Save polygon coordinates on the two stacks using the File–Save As–XY Coordinates tool.
Extract motion trajectories from the focused stack using ImageJ’s Particle Tracker plugin.
Set Radius to 3 in the Particle Detection part of the Particle Tracker dialog screen.
Set Cutoff to 0 in the Particle Detection part.
Set Percentile between 0 and 5 depending on the total intensity of the stack and particle density in the Particle Detection part.
Preview detected particles in other frames using the Preview Detected button and slider.
Set Displacement to 2 or 3 in the Particle Linking part.
Set Link Range to 2 or 3 in the Particle Linking part.
Calculate the transformation matrix between two planes using simple matrix operations.
Transform xy coordinates of the trajectory on the focus plane to the defocus plane using the calculated transformation matrix.
Create a subfolder named “Image” to store diffraction ring images.
Read the image in file “Dec” frame by frame for each trajectory, and store intensity values in an intensity matrix I0.
Define a square region of interest (ROI) with a side length of 31 pixels.
For the kth point on the trajectory, obtain the value of the intensity matrix I0 centered at (xk, yk).
Convert the ROI matrix to a grayscale image and save it named “ith track kth frame” in the folder “Image”.
Calculate the radius of the diffraction ring using MATLAB.
Read the ROI image frame by frame for each trajectory and store in a matrix I.
Apply a real-space bandpass filter to obtain a matrix I1 with an improved signal-to-noise ratio.
Set an appropriate threshold to binarize matrix I1 and save it as a new matrix I2.
Use the circleHough function to obtain the radius r0 of the binary image.
Perform fitting to the matrix I1 using a Gaussian peak surrounded by a ring equation.
Set initial values for fitting and select the result with the largest R-square value.
Save the frame number, xy coordinates, and radius of each track in an array.
Plot the radius as a function of frame number for each trajectory.
Use the brush tool to remove discontinuous points from the array.
Determine the calibration between the ring radius and z position.
Use the multipoint tool in the defocus plane to select the center position of the diffraction ring directly.
Save the image stack as an image sequence to a folder named “Def” using the File–Save As–Image Sequence tool.
Import the position of the diffraction ring to MATLAB.
Repeat steps 29f-29j to save the ring images.
Calculate the ring radius.
Plot the radius as a function of frame number.
Obtain the averaged value of each step with the getline function.
Linearly fit the value with the z position of the piezo stage using cftool.
Multiply the ring radius by the slope of the calibration to obtain the axial coordinates (z).
For fixed points on the glass, repeat steps 26-30 to obtain the xy coordinates and radius.
Calculate the localization precision for a fixed point where MSD = 2*σ^2 in each direction, σ being the localization precision.
Randomly select 10 fixed points.
Calculate the average MSD curve in the xyz three directions to determine the localization precision.
Calculate the z-coordinate of the trajectory from the ring radius obtained previously and the calibration.
Reconstruct a complete 3D trajectory with xyz coordinates over time.
Select trajectories with track lengths longer than 50 frames for analysis.
Calculate the mean squared displacement (MSD) curve using the equation MSD(τ) = |r(t + τ) − r(t)|², where r is the 3D coordinates and τ is the lag time.
Calculate the mean squared displacement between all point locations in each direction (x, y, z) with a time interval of n*0.03 s for n=1 to 33 frames.
Fit the MSD curve to the lag time to calculate the diffusion coefficient and anomalous exponents.
Plot the MSD of each trajectory as a function of lag time in log-log scale.
Observe if the MSD curve is a straight line or a curve.
Fit dynamic parameters directly from the entire curve if the MSD curve is a straight line.
Fit parameters separately at different time scales if the MSD curve changes at different time scales.
